title: Client-rendered Vite + React app whose initial HTML is an empty shell
declared_defects: Every captured route is served as an app shell: an empty div#root, a module script, a stylesheet, and a short noscript note. The marketing shell (captures/app-shell.raw.html) carries 19 words of visible text and the handbook shell (captures/handbook-shell.raw.html) carries 23, while the rendered documents carry several hundred each. Every page therefore trips the word-count arm of content-in-initial-html: the initial response holds well under half the rendered text and the shortfall is far above 100 words (SEO-593).

Neither shell declares a <title>. document.title is assigned inside the effect in src/lib/useDocumentHead.js, so all three routes have a title that exists only after client-side execution — a second, separate content-in-initial-html finding on each page (SEO-593).

Neither shell contains an <h1>. The heading is rendered by the route component, so all three routes have a page heading that appears only after client-side execution — a third content-in-initial-html finding on each page (SEO-593).

index.html declares no canonical at all. useDocumentHead appends one after mount, so on / and /features the canonical exists only for consumers that execute scripts: client-mutates-canonical reports an addition on each of those two pages (SEO-597).

handbook.html hard-codes <link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/handbook">, the section root, and useDocumentHead rewrites that element's href to the article's own URL. /handbook/routing therefore serves one canonical before execution and a different one after, which is the mutation arm of client-mutates-canonical (SEO-597).
notes:
This is the fixture that proves the two JavaScript-rendering checks work, so it is the only one where raw_html and rendered_html are deliberately different documents. Everything else about the rendered captures is clean on purpose: one title, one meta description, one absolute self-referencing canonical, a complete Open Graph set including og:url and og:image:alt, a JSON-LD @graph whose WebSite and Organization nodes carry distinct @id values, and images with alt text and declared dimensions. If any of those were defective the fixture would emit findings unrelated to rendering and the benchmark could no longer attribute a finding to the defect that caused it. Because every check except the two rendering checks reads `rendered_html ?? raw_html`, those 20 checks are inspecting the rendered documents and reaching PASS, which is why they are listed under expected_non_findings.

The project ships public/robots.txt rather than a root robots.txt because that is where a Vite project puts it; loadSnapshot's robots discovery is depth-agnostic (it takes the shallowest match for /(^|\/)robots\.txt$/), so the file is found there. It deliberately ships no sitemap.xml, no llms.txt, and no feed, so the five sitemap checks, robots-sitemap-reference, the two llms.txt checks, and the two feed checks all report NOT_APPLICABLE. That is honest for an app that cannot serve its own content as HTML, and per the honesty rule those NOT_APPLICABLE checks are not padded into expected_non_findings. The three hreflang checks and jsonld-review-without-source are NOT_APPLICABLE for the same reason: nothing declares hreflang and nothing carries review markup.

source_file points at the route component rather than at index.html because raw and rendered differ, which means location() emits a bare path with no line number, and the route module is the file a person actually has to change: the content, the heading, and the head metadata all live there. The two marketing pages share one raw capture file because Vite serves a single entry document for both routes, so the served bytes really are identical.

expected_blocked names SEO-593 and SEO-597, the two requirements this fixture's findings bind to; both are REVIEW_REQUIRED in the registry, which is what stops an agent from turning "we found it" into "so we rewrote the build". expected_safe_fixes names SEO-033 and SEO-034 because the narrow remedy for the shell's missing title and description — static tags in index.html — is SAFE_AUTOMATIC in the registry and is a different piece of work from pre-rendering the routes.

No expected_not_applicable assertions here. Registry-selection negative tests belong to the monolingual static marketing fixture (vite-static), where the profile facts that gate them are settled; this fixture is scoped to the rendering axis.
expected_applicable_rationale: This fixture is the positive half of the JavaScript-rendering pair, and every one of these rules is gated on client_rendered or javascript_app or has_router - facts the project establishes for real by shipping one empty shell and a client router. Asserting them here is what makes the twelve findings falsifiable: a rule that was never offered could not have been reported, so proving the offer is a precondition for trusting the report.
